Details:
Communist organizers turn propaganda networks and local agitation into control of vulnerable states. As their foothold deepens, agitation can harden into insurgent strongholds and lockdowns, raising the risk of revolt.

Governments can intervene locally or launch a broader emergency response. Delay gives the movement more chances to spread, stage unexpected uprisings, and draw the country toward revolution.
Evo I: Communist cells turn local unrest into sudden revolts. Strikes, clandestine committees, and armed breakaways make every communist-held district a possible center of insurrection.
Evo II: Worker circles gather after dark in mills, mines, and depots, binding revolutionary discipline to secret rites. Fear spreads through industrial districts as the movement gains new converts.
Evo III: Lockdown zones speak of one world revolution and treat distant uprisings as parts of the same struggle. Their whispers prepare new strongholds for a conflict that no border can contain.
World-End Scenario: No terminal world-end. Whispers of the World Revolution hands the communist crisis to the separate World Revolution major event, where controlled states may become revolutionary bases.

Details:
A zombie outbreak erupts in a populous state and grows by consuming the people and territory in its path. Crowded, underdeveloped regions face the greatest risk of secondary outbreaks, while each evolution makes the horde harder to contain.

Countries can fortify the front, reduce outbreak risk, pursue a cure, and coordinate through the Anti-Zombie League. If the horde gains momentum, it can spread faster than isolated governments can respond.
Evo I: The first major adaptation lets the horde endure hunger and darkness. Early containment lines begin to fail as the dead keep moving through nights that once slowed them.
Evo II: A faster strain drives the horde into sustained assaults. Starved packs cross broken supply lines without losing their pace, and laboratories struggle to keep the cure abreast of the mutation.
Evo III: The final mutation makes the horde exceptionally difficult to exhaust or cure. Weak fronts can collapse under attacks that continue through darkness, isolation, and ruined supply routes.
World-End Scenario:
Zombie Apocalypse

The outbreak has outgrown every line built to contain it. The dead move from ruined cities into the last organized refuges, while the living lose the roads, laboratories, and armies needed to answer them.

The Zombie Horde becomes the dominant order of the world. Isolated survivors remain in scattered refuges under a world ordered by the dead.

Wendigo Ascendancy

The engineered Wendigo outbreak has crossed every remaining continental threshold. Packs take the last organized territories and open a world ruled by predation and permanent winter.

Details: A Himalayan refuge can become the Holy Realm as its people develop a Bodhisattva-led order, the Arhat Administration, and the Buddha Mandate. Political and spiritual choices shape whether the state follows restraint, peacekeeping, coercive pacification, Divine Sovereignty, or the final doctrine.
Evo I: Repeated teachings under chaos pressure make suffering itself the Realm's central proof. Ruined roads, frightened capitals, and broken armies are treated as evidence that mercy must answer the crisis directly.
Evo II: The Relic Mandala carries the Realm's vows beyond its own mountains. Pilgrim routes, foreign seats, and guarded relic lines turn distant states into a sacred network.
Evo III: A schism appears when high Defilements corrupt the path toward Buddhahood. Teaching can purify the rupture. Suppression can turn the wound into another source of power.
Evo IV: Awakened protection answered the Sun and Moon crisis. The Realm remembers it as the strongest public proof that its powers can turn against chaos.
World-End Scenario: The Holy Realm completes its last rite and launches the Final Silence strikes. The last sanctuaries are destroyed, governments collapse, and the Awakened One leaves the Empty Seat to guard what survives.

Details: Wars erupt between eligible countries and expand into linked conflict webs as chaos rises. Special countries can join later stages, turning a local declaration into a wider chain of fighting.
Evo I: One declaration draws a third country into the dispute. Mobilization orders cross in transit, and a local quarrel becomes a triangular war before diplomats can separate the claims.
Evo II: Retaliatory declarations open four connected fronts. Opportunists enter the fighting, border commands choose their own enemies, and the original dispute disappears beneath a wider war.
Evo III: Ultimatums pass from capital to capital until major powers and faction partners join the crisis. Each new belligerent brings another grievance and another border into the fighting.
Evo IV: A week of declarations binds six countries into one conflict web. Strange powers and old rivals seize the opening, turning hurried mobilization into a war across several regions.
Evo V: Governments abandon the last restraint on opportunistic war. Declarations spread across the world in rapid succession, and every exposed border becomes a possible front.

Details:
The Soviet Union is losing command over its republics, rail offices, garrisons, and depots. Moscow can answer with force, negotiation, isolation, or party discipline, but each visible failure gives local authorities more room to act.

Free Republics' League: [GetEventsLogSovietCollapseDetailLeague]
Moscow Authority: [GetEventsLogSovietCollapseDetailAuthority]
Union Crisis Threat: [GetEventsLogSovietCollapseDetailThreat]
Foreign intervention: [GetEventsLogSovietCollapseDetailForeign]
Old movements and splinters: [GetEventsLogSovietCollapseDetailMutation]

Forced-labor quotas, grain extraction, and NKVD campaigns can briefly reinforce Moscow's authority, but each use deepens famine pressure, republic fear, old-movement grievance, and the evidence record. Once the crisis becomes severe, repression can no longer reduce the terminal threat.

Breakaway republics can seek recognition, seize depots, coordinate defenses, or draw more republics into the crisis while Moscow tries to restore command or force a new settlement.
Evo I: A republic ministry, garrison, or depot network stops obeying Moscow and survives long enough to make its independence visible. The first durable break gives every other separatist a precedent.
Evo II: Several republics are free, and the example spreads through foreign recognition, weak depots, League coordination, and public refusal. Secession becomes a regional current rather than an isolated revolt.
Evo III: Moscow has lost command across the Union. The remaining republics leave the old center, and the former Union enters open war over its borders and inheritance.
Evo IV: The last republics and stranger splinter movements break into the open. Armies, ministries, and local councils compete to inherit territory, weapons, and authority from the former Union.
Evo V:
World Collapse Rupture

The rupture reaches every surviving remnant. The former Union becomes one front among a collapsing world as its last claimants fight over identities and borders that no center can enforce.

Fringe Breakaways

Fringe claimants and stranger offices are breaking from the former Union as maximum collapse pressure gives them room to become governments.

Details:
New governments have taken control of capitals, ministries, and borders across several regions. They must secure recognition, administration, defense, and settlements with former hosts and foreign patrons. Former hosts retain part of their territory. A surviving country that loses at least [?constant:independence_wave_join.reduction_percent|0]% of its former states and at least [?constant:independence_wave_join.minimum_states_lost|0] states may join the wave if every retained state belongs to one prepared homeland.

[GetIndependenceWaveRivalBlocEventDetails]
[GetIndependenceWaveRivalBlocEventDetailsMember]
Evo I: Founding charters, civil-service manuals, recognition protocols, and trusted couriers now pass from one young state to the next. New governments enter the world with stronger institutions, earlier diplomatic contacts, and a network prepared to sponsor their survival.
Evo II: Dormant national projects and half-remembered unions return to political life. Regional and signature independence movements can surface sooner, while the states already born from the wave gain the confidence and institutions needed to rediscover larger identities.
Evo III: The next declarations arrive with officers, guarded depots, and plans for immediate defense. Breakaway governments gain stronger military budgets and better prepared forces, but every rifle issued sharpens instability, former-host hostility, and the fear of reconquest.
Evo IV: The informal network becomes a congress of delegates, observers, and rejected clients. Recognition missions, arbitration, rescue commitments, and a shared reserve draw the independent states toward collective leadership without deciding the charter they must ultimately choose.
Evo V: World collapse strips old borders of their final authority. New sovereignty projects enter the struggle for independence, while existing breakaways gain the freedom and pressure to pursue dangerous routes.

Details:
An unnatural rage seizes a minor country and turns it into a rogue war state. Fury columns gather supplies and reinforcements, then attack neighboring countries as conquest feeds the violence.

The crisis can harden the first Fury state, ignite rival or allied outbreaks, and end in simultaneous wars across every available border.
Evo I: The first Fury state learns to sustain its rage. Columns regroup around captured depots, hardened commanders drive them farther, and neighboring countries face an enemy that no longer burns itself out in one campaign.
Evo II: A second Fury state takes the field. The two hosts may share enemies, compete for plunder, or attack one another, leaving the countries between them exposed to wars on several fronts.
Evo III: Fury spreads among several states, and their armies strike across every reachable border. Separate rampages merge into a continental war in which rage decides policy and peace has no constituency.
World-End Scenario:
Fury is no longer confined to one rogue state. Armed hosts answer one another across continents, each treating the nearest border as an invitation to attack and every pause as weakness.

A network of Fury states opens a global war without a negotiated political end. Rage becomes the world's governing order.

Details: Public accusations, leaked cables, and military bulletins unsettle foreign offices before any government admits that a crisis exists. In calmer periods the alarm chiefly raises international tension. As chaos deepens, repeated incidents poison relations, quicken later crises, push governments toward readiness, and may turn a disputed frontier into a limited clash.
Evo I: Cable traffic swells as embassies answer rumours with denials. Relations begin to fray, and each new dispatch makes the next alarm easier to believe.
Evo II: Competing accusations spread through more capitals. Delayed reports keep old suspicions alive, while cautious governments quietly raise their readiness.
Evo III: General staffs begin treating rumour as operational guidance. Diplomatic shocks linger, frontier incidents become harder to contain, and governments watch the Thin Wire with growing unease.
Evo IV: Extended alert becomes the normal condition. Heavier accusations and exhausted border commands make a limited frontier clash more likely as the border grows harder to control.

Details:
Exhausted belligerents accept peace without conquest or indemnity, restoring the borders they held before the war. Early settlements close a single war between minor countries.

As the event evolves, several minor wars can end together, major powers may rarely be included, and a wider diplomatic settlement can quiet a world crowded with wars.
Evo I: Minor belligerents begin accepting armistices that restore the old frontier. Several small wars can end together as exhausted governments abandon claims that no longer justify the cost.
Evo II: A major power may accept a settlement without land or tribute when neither side can secure a decisive result. The wider struggle continues, but one costly front falls silent.
Evo III: Armistice envoys carry the same settlement across several unrelated fronts. Governments set aside disputed gains, reopen crossings, and release armies trapped in wars that no longer serve them.

Details:
Death begins in silence on a remote island. Ships stop returning, settlements empty, and the Black Ledger reaches toward other islands before turning to the mainland.

Every state Death consumes is emptied of its people and reduced to a wasteland. The dead feed Death's soul power, which it spends to spread, raise ghost hosts, and open new footholds. Retaking land does not restore it, and survivors must invest in making the dead zones usable again.

Living countries can investigate the disappearances, guard their coasts, build quarantine lines, join the Living Compact, and prepare troops for the wastelands. Death is defeated only when every state under its control has been reclaimed.
Evo I: Death reaches a second island and empties it slowly enough to resemble lost shipping or an abandoned harbor. The silence spreads from shore to shore while mainland governments remain uncertain of its cause.
Evo II: The Black Ledger reaches the mainland. Coastal settlements empty, survivors name the force consuming them, and the first organized war against Death begins.
Evo III: Weak ghost hosts rise from emptied land and gather along its borders. They defend the wasteland in broken ranks while Death prepares a larger army from those it has counted.
Evo IV: The hollow hosts return in greater numbers and hold their ranks longer. They remain imperfect soldiers, yet every fallen district gives Death more ground from which to raise them.
Evo V: An emptied continent becomes Death's muster ground. Ghost hosts cross the last shores in force and attack the living wherever the Black Ledger remains unfinished.
World-End Scenario:
Death has emptied enough land to turn islands, wastelands, and ghost hosts into one design. A consumed continent gives Zol the ground from which to reach every surviving shore.

New footholds open across the living world, and the dead march from the last shores to complete the Black Ledger. No population remains beyond Death's count.

Details: A covert alliance leaves the same traces in distant incidents. Couriers vanish, equipment fails, and quiet methods recur across borders. Following the pattern can expose the network before its next operation.
Evo I: The same routes, tricks, and timings appear far beyond the first incidents. Leaks and defections expose fragments of a hidden partnership whose full membership remains unknown.
Evo II: Covert attacks across several countries now follow one plan. Governments hunt for the alliance behind the campaign as agents sabotage defenses and deepen suspicion between possible partners.
Evo III: Border pressure and military preparations bring the hidden alliance close to open confrontation. Its members maneuver for the first blow while exposed countries prepare for a war whose sides are still unclear.

Details: An African government has started pulling the continent together with aid, guarantees, liberation deals, and a common Charter. Other countries can join, bargain, walk away, or build a rival camp. If the project keeps its promises, regional congresses and constitutional settlements can turn the idea into roads, armies, laws, and a fierce argument over who carries the cost.
Evo I: The Charter League has kept its first promise and can finally look beyond one corridor. Regional congresses, negotiated settlements, restoration claims, and rival blocs will decide whether its protection grows into lasting cooperation.
Evo II: The League is settling into daily life. Shared railways, emergency forces, membership law, and resource bargains tie distant courts together, and every new connection brings another bill or obligation.
Evo III: Africa's settlement has become a question every great power must answer. Foreign bases, sanctions, continent-wide mobilization, strange new actors, and rival projects are now part of the same struggle.
World-End Scenario: The African Union has absorbed or defeated every rival government. It proclaims The World, binds the surviving territories to one constitutional order, and ends the age of separate states.

Details: Rivers burst their banks, faults split open, storms tear through rail lines, ash buries farms, and wildfires outrun the roads. Each disaster leaves a local fight to rescue survivors, steady the region, and rebuild before the next emergency arrives.
Evo I: Bad seasons bring several disasters close together. Rescue crews, supplies, and safe roads become harder to share when every region seems to need them at once.
Evo II: The damage spills across state lines. Broken transport, hunger, disease, refugees, and exhausted reconstruction crews turn one ruined region into a problem for all its neighbors.
Evo III: The disasters begin moving in impossible ways. Ruptures, meteors, ash clouds, storms, tornadoes, and tsunamis travel across whole regions, giving countries only a rough idea of where the next blow will land.

Details:
Burial parties vanish from an army at war. Ration books are quietly changed, bodies are cut apart, and frightened soldiers whisper that officers are protecting the people responsible.

The army must feed its units, protect witnesses, and hunt organized killers without turning the whole front into a panic. Covering up the crimes keeps order briefly and gives the predators room to recruit.
Evo I: Scattered predators now share oaths, marks, ranks, and protection. The cells recognize one another, though nobody can find a headquarters.
Evo II: Cells in different countries use the same ledgers, courier routes, prisoner rules, and attack schedules. The network is clearly organized, but its center is still hidden.
Evo III: A concealed command steps into public view and begins drawing the mature network into one campaign.
World-End Scenario:
The World Is the Larder

The unified Host has pulled the feeding territories and armed kitchens into one command. Roads, farms, prisons, and conquered cities are all treated as parts of the same larder. Surviving countries are reduced to prey, raiders, or small resistance enclaves.

The network has no reason to hide anymore. Every government still standing faces an expanding Host that intends to feed on the whole world.

No Thaw Will Come

The Winter Host has given itself to the Wendigo hunger. Feeding grounds spread with the cold, and conquered communities are dragged into a world where thaw, harvest, and mercy are treated as weaknesses.

Winter advances with the Host. Every surviving country is hunted until human rule is consumed or driven into a handful of frozen refuges.

Details: A translated manifesto slips out of reading rooms and into the government of a small country. It promises that common stores, useful work, and public need can build a fairer society. Its readers divide over who decides what people need and how much freedom the plan can afford. Shortages, public works, local charters, and deals with neighbors put every promise to the test.
Evo I: Everyone has started writing in the manifesto's margins. Workers, parishes, councils, families, and exiles bring their own copies and their own answers. The movement's future may belong to whoever keeps the right to edit the book.
Evo II: Migration, blockades, crowded homes, and thin supplies push the common store to its limits. Surveyors search for harbors, corridors, settlements, and leases that can meet real needs without turning the commonwealth into a hungry neighbor.
Evo III: The plan has escaped the capital. Towns and rebuilt districts are opening gardens, clinics, workshops, stores, and transport links of their own. Local votes and local shortages shape each version, and arguments over work reveal who really gets to change the plan.
Evo IV: The manifesto now has a place in regional politics. Governments quote it when they ask for aid, defend local charters, refuse threats, or seek association. Small states must decide whether the commonwealth looks like a refuge, a useful partner, or an ambitious neighbor.
Evo V: The world around the commonwealth is coming apart. Reserve trains, guarded harbors, refugee districts, fortifications, and member councils all compete for the same supplies. One path closes the gates and demands service from everyone inside. The other shares refuge among willing towns and spreads the burden across the league.

Details:
Doctor Warren Kruger arrives with working results in fields that rarely fit inside one career, much less one mind. A government can hire him openly, place him inside a secret military programme, or point his talents somewhere else. Wherever he settles, universities, factories, armies, and foreign spies gather around the same guarded rooms.

Kruger's laboratory soon becomes an institution with secrets and ambitions of its own. Everyone accepts that he is brilliant. The government must still prove it can command what his brilliance creates.

The D’Rhondan landings have produced a sovereign exile state whose scattered enclaves remember another world. Its leaders must preserve their people, settle their place on Earth, and decide what they owe to the countries beneath their landing grounds.
Evo I: Kruger's laboratory has become part of national life. His methods are spreading through universities, factories, hospitals, and military planning.
Evo II: Foreign governments are courting Kruger, copying his work, and sending people to steal it. The scientific race is becoming a struggle between states.
Evo III: The Directorate is repeating experiments that ordinary ministries can barely understand, much less supervise. Every dangerous success draws more people and facilities into Kruger's private network.
Evo IV: Kruger has stopped asking permission. He arrives with a demand for political authority and the backing of laboratories, staff, and machines that answer to him.
World-End Scenario:
Laboratory World

Kruger's Directorate has swallowed the governments that once tried to supervise it. Countries, populations, and whole landscapes survive as controlled samples inside a planetary laboratory.

The world has become one experiment, and Kruger alone decides what happens to the control group.

The Strategic Singularity

The Directorate's final device tears through armies, cities, and the air itself. The blast leaves mass death, poisoned ground, and governments too broken to hold the old world together.

The Singularity ends Kruger's experiment and leaves the survivors in a world of fallout.

Details: A small neutral country is running out of room to stand alone. The great blocs offer protection, weapons, and a seat at their table, sending their envoys toward the next exposed border. Neutrality becomes a political and military struggle fought through councils, troops, and public resolve.
Evo I: One accession starts a regional scramble. Border guards dig in, observers arrive, neutrality councils meet, and faction officers make themselves comfortable in nearby capitals.
Evo II: War makes neutrality harder to sell. Countries beside active fronts receive sharper demands, louder promises, and less time to answer.
Evo III: Several small states can be pulled toward rival blocs in quick succession. The last neutral capitals answer with hurried councils, guarded borders, and expensive promises to stand alone.

Details: Surveyors have struck a major deposit in one of the country's states. The first find promises jobs, trade, and new industry. Repeated discoveries can turn the same field into a boomtown, a diplomatic prize, or something much harder to control.
Evo I: One field keeps giving. New deposits appear beneath old workings, and foreign buyers, rival claimants, and would-be peacekeepers all want a share of the wealth.
Evo II: Miners fall sick, metal corrodes overnight, people vanish, and something attacks in the lower workings. The country must investigate, contain the danger, or close the field before the boomtown becomes a grave.
Evo III: A huge mixed deposit pulls the workings far below safe ground. Attacks reach the surface, and the country must hunt what escaped, evacuate the field, or seal away every valuable shaft before the breach fully opens.
Evo IV: The field opens into an Oth-Kesh origin chamber. Armored broods pour through the workings, feed on rich deposits, and attack every country they can reach as they search for roads beneath the next continent.
World-End Scenario:
The Oth-Kesh have secured their first continent and opened new chambers beyond the sea. The tunnels below become roads for armored broods, and fresh fronts tear open beneath the richest ground.

Every surviving continent now has its own entrance to the World Below. The surface is caught in one global war against the depths.

Details:
Fully formed military units are appearing across the world with no recruitment orders, training records, or known home. Governments suddenly have to feed, equip, command, and watch soldiers who arrived ready to march.

Some formations bring strange weapons, ambitious commanders, or troops that are not human at all. A useful windfall can become a rival army very quickly.
Evo I: The soldiers from nowhere now have district staffs, proper rolls, and officers the government can actually hold responsible.
Evo II: New formations arrive carrying baffling mixes of weapons and gear. Each one needs its own training, spare parts, and supply plan.
Evo III: Some new commanders inspire more loyalty than the government that received them. Their private authority can split an army or put a claimant in the capital.
Evo IV: Not every arriving host is human. Governments must decide whether to quarter these soldiers, bargain with them, or turn them away before an armed camp becomes a country of its own.

Details:
A black-marked fever has broken out on the mainland. It moves through roads, ports, hungry cities, and rat-filled ruins, leaving governments to choose which places to isolate and which people they can still save.

If the plague is allowed to settle in, the rats may become something more dangerous than carriers. Whole warrens can learn to fight, govern, and follow a king of their own.
Evo I: The plague has learned to thrive in crowded and poorly protected places. Deaths rise faster, and every untreated corridor helps the next wave spread.
Evo II: Ports and long-distance transport carry the plague beyond its mainland cradle. Docks, troop convoys, refugees, and wartime shipping can open a second front across the sea.
Evo III: Collapsed plague basins have joined one Rat Nation. Its broods seize infected ground and build armies without human soldiers or ordinary equipment.
Evo IV: A royal basin has learned to obey one sentient ruler. The Rat King gathers memory, hunger, and authority as the surviving broods decide whether to kneel.
Evo V: The Rat King's dominion has grown beyond the warrens. Capitals fall silent, refuges are overrun, and the last continental cordons begin to break.
World-End Scenario: The Rat King rules from the Royal Basin, where the plague's surviving broods gather under one crown. Fallen capitals and overrun refuges feed a kingdom that carries its warrens, human servants, and royal hunger across the world.

Details: A random country fractures into rival governments and armed camps.
A violent antisemitic faction emerges during the Spanish Civil War, seeks an alliance with Nazi Germany, and threatens Jewish communities across Europe.
Soviet scientists secretly develop nuclear weapons before the wider world expects them.
A Swedish war game movement grants its divisions new tactical training and battlefield advantages.
A race for alien technology in Antarctica can unlock advanced jet research for the country that secures the site.
A government considers moving industry into the desert to preserve living space on the mainland.
A major country gains a complete military doctrine after a sudden research breakthrough.

Scientists track a large asteroid and race to predict its impact. A correct prediction brings a research windfall, while an unexpected strike destroys industry and kills people in the affected states.
A chance discovery brings a country a large political windfall and turns one state into a source of continuing income.

A time traveler known as “Time Traveler” advises a country and warns certain governments against wars that history says they will lose. A later route can bring Napoleon back, followed by a robot invasion from the future.
Evo I: Time Traveler: a historical warning system guides governments away from wars that history says they will lose.
Evo IV: Napoleon returns (Pretzel Logic), World End scenario: army of robots from the future invade, basically like in the movie Terminator.

Details: Violence erupts in a random country, damaging buildings and killing civilians.
Missile technology spreads across the world.
Acid rain crosses continents, reducing populations and damaging affected states.
A random major country enters an industrial boom and doubles its production efficiency.
A major country is hit by a deep economic downturn.
A country recovers an alien spacecraft and receives a fleet of jet fighters plus the means to produce more.
A major country receives millions of unexplained new recruits.
Malta becomes independent, raises knightly armies, claims Mediterranean territory, and wages a new crusade. Later stages can place the Pope in Rome at the head of a Kingdom of God.
Evo IV: A dedicated crusader route opens. Failure leads to an eleventh crusade, while success expands the conquests, adopts The Holy See identity, installs the Pope as leader, and makes Rome the holy capital of a Kingdom of God.

Details: A random country's leader is murdered, leaving the government to face a succession crisis.
A random Arabian country falls under British control through a Lawrence of Arabia intervention.
A mysterious shipment falls from the sky, changing a country's military prospects.
A country receives a sudden shipment of military equipment.
A massive flood devastates every coastal state it reaches.
The major powers enter a race to reach space.
The Balkan states plunge into a third regional war.
No active earthquake scenario is available for this event.
A mysterious explosion destroys a random province and may resemble a nuclear strike.
Bulgaria revives claims over its historic lands.
A mad scientist's warning spreads mass panic through the country.
A major country is cut off by a global embargo.
A heat wave sweeps across the world as a separate crisis.
A major country's intelligence becomes exposed to every government.
A sudden scientific breakthrough spreads across the world.
A country enters a sudden infrastructure boom.
A naval renaissance gives every country a functioning fleet.
Radar coverage expands across the world.
Industry expands in every country as factories spread with the territory under control.
Every country expands its civilian industry in proportion to the territory it controls.
Every country adopts a more aggressive strategic posture.
A research setback leaves a nation with only two research slots. A Kruger Directorate can preserve its current capacity at a concrete political and institutional cost.
Half of each country's military factories become civilian factories.
A faction expels a random member and declares war on it.
A random puppet breaks free and becomes independent.
Country leaders develop unexpected talents.
Every country leader receives a random trait.
International market funding expands for a random major country.
A random country elevates one general to the rank of Generalissimo and gives him exceptional ability.
People from another universe called ZIN settle in a state and its neighbors. They claim neutrality, yet a war against them unleashes a supernatural reprisal.
Evo IV: Later waves bring several alien invasions, each with a distinct weakness.

Details: A Boxer Rebellion erupts in China.
African gods predict a world consumed by chaos. Prayer can delay disasters, while neglect makes each wave faster and more destructive until the campaign faces ruin.
Iran restores the Persian Empire and attacks every country holding Persian cores.
Ireland attacks the holder of Northern Ireland. The conflict can end when Ireland secures the region.
Mongolia revives a steppe empire, gains claims on its neighbors, and raises large cavalry forces.
Japan seizes California during its war with the United States.
Tannu Tuva joins the Allies or God's Plan when that faction exists.
The United States tests new weapons in another country's territory.
A major country or the player sends stored equipment to a random minor ally.
A border conflict erupts between the player and a random neighbor.
A hidden master pressures a random minor country to follow a rival or opposing ideology.
A giant tourist airship leaves the United States on a round-the-world voyage. If it crashes, the United States gains a war goal and the impact can damage the state or start a wildfire.
Britain imposes taxes on every country.
Every country moves one step toward total mobilization.
A sudden windfall places political power in every government.
A surge of military experience raises every country's commanders.
Every country receives 100 army, navy, or air experience of its chosen type.
Germany or the Soviet Union proclaims a claim to the world.
A temporary military emergency boosts entrenchment across the world.
Governments form technology-sharing networks.
Kamikaze doctrine spreads to every country.
Every country gains access to kamikaze strikes.

Lenin returns with a third eye and an army of humanoid workers. The revolution spreads through states in proportion to communist support, while defecting communists gain power and slowly become part of the monster host. Stalin and Trotsky fight Lenin as the movement grows.
Evo IV: Strange worker strikes foreshadow Lenin's return. Later stages expose the anomalous forces, strengthen Lenin's powers, and draw communist leaders into the transformation.

Details: Countries compete to buy Greenland.
Portugal demands Galicia from Spain.
A random major country or the player loses half of its equipment stockpiles.
An exiled country launches a revolt from occupied territory. When no occupation exists, a dormant claimant can appear before any war begins.
Division templates become temporarily unavailable to every country.
Countries establish collaboration networks against one another.
A country discovers a new metal that improves armor production in the state it controls. Other governments can seek access to the resource through agreements.
A Dust and Sandstorm crisis reaches the selected country once Wider Disaster Seasons is available. This entry uses the Natural Disasters event family.
Inflation grips major countries and the player. Stability rises or falls with the crisis, and a prolonged failure can bring political upheaval or civil war.
Countries face timed tasks whose failure brings harmful consequences.
A serial killer terrorizes a country through a chain of murders. The investigation follows a chain of choices, and a mistake sends it back to the beginning.
Low war support pushes conscription downward, while strong war support enables higher conscription.
Each country weighs stability against war support, gaining one while sacrificing the other.
A player's ideology faces temporary decline and public discontent. Protest movements are weaker when support is high, while a collapse below one percent can trigger regime change or civil war.
A paranoia crisis spreads through a country in a manner similar to the Soviet Union crisis.
A random rule becomes active and changes the campaign.
A small non-island country launches an expansionist campaign.
A new national spirit appears in every country.
Occupied states erupt in resistance across major countries and the player.
A chest market introduces common, rare, and epic prizes to a country's political life.
A national wrestling tournament turns one contender into a public hero.
A wrestling tournament rewards the champion after countries train their chosen contender.
A worldwide fuel crisis leaves every country with no stored fuel.
A Macedonian uprising turns the slogan Freedom or Death into a national crisis.
Spartan warriors rise in Greece.
A major country or the player faces five rival camps in a civil war. Stability and ideology support shape the opening balance, while alliances can postpone the final duel.
A plague of locusts travels across the world and brings famine to affected regions.
A new regional alliance forms in a random part of the world.
A massive volcanic eruption turns the states around a random volcanic region into wasteland.
The strongest country in a random ideology proposes a pact in which every member guarantees the others.
Cossacks rise from a random East Slavic state and expand across East Slavia.
Several neighbors claim a random country and divide its territory or fight for it.
Countries at peace demilitarize every state except their capital until war allows remilitarization.
Two random countries sign a non-aggression pact.
A religious faction forms with the goal of destroying rival religions.
Subject governments demand greater autonomy.
Every subject receives autonomy points.
A regional shaman offers aid to the major country that controls the surrounding area.
Tomorrow's Girls brings alien companions into national politics, and a leader can gain manpower through their influence.
Countries with low war support face army mutinies as units turn against their commands.
A government invests in military, civilian, naval, or special industry.

Countries holding non-core states face independence movements shaped by Gandhi's principles of nonviolence, noncooperation, truth, and honesty. Denial removes the value of occupation while unrest spreads, with fascist governments affected differently.
Countries face a sudden surplus of military equipment.
Every country receives a choice of large equipment grants.
A research surge focuses each country on one field.
Every country receives a choice of research investment in one category.
A mountain and hill country forms the Mountain Republic and claims every matching state.
A creature feeds on crops and people in a random major country or the player, spreading fear until it is hunted.

Dracula terrorizes Transylvania and can found the Vampire Kingdom, which attacks its former controller and England before threatening the world. The one-battalion “Count Dracula” unit decides the kingdom's fate, and neighbors receive the “Fear of Dracula” national spirit until they confront it.
Whispers drive mass suicides in a random major country or the player. As deaths spread, generals and leaders can disappear until the country itself collapses.
A major country or player with strong ideological support faces partisan divisions, some of them armored, in proportion to its support.
A rock-paper-scissors contest decides a territorial dispute. Victory transfers the state, while defeat costs part of the player's industry.
Subjects across the world declare independence and form the National Liberation Front. Their former masters can accept the separation or fight the simultaneous wars.
Intelligence agencies expand their clandestine networks.
Counterintelligence improves across the world.
Every country gains one point of counterintelligence.
Pacifism rises again as a political force.
Retired and absorbed into the shared dynamic famine and migration system. Unavailable as a random event.

A shadowy society known as “Secret Society Influence” affects a government's ministers and generals, causing confusion and distrust. The national spirit reduces stability and political power while increasing consumer goods demand.
A teleportation experiment makes one division vanish. A later breakthrough can move several divisions and shorten the cooldown.
Evo IV: A teleportation breakthrough moves multiple divisions and shortens the cooldown.

Details: A conspiracy-theorist movement forms.
A random major country guarantees a random minor.
New Zealand begins questioning its own existence.
A prophet travels the world preaching peace, leaving sayings in every country he visits.
A travelling man reaches the United States and leaves behind a series of disruptive events.
Every country moves its capital to a random state.
An alien invasion begins through the mysterious song "Tomorrow's Girls" by Donald Fagen. A social game asks whether each girl is human or alien.
A vision of a unified world of salads and sun spreads across the campaign.
Shark-infested waters increase casualties whenever ships sink.
The Devil offers power in exchange for escalating bargains. Accepting more deals deepens the demonic influence, while refusal can bring new offers and harsher consequences before the pact is broken.
Evo IV: The demonic influence reaches a second visual stage, with the leader's eyes changing.

Details: Alien fears lead the United States to form an anti-alien coalition, with its leader adopting a tinfoil hat.
A mysterious doctor appears with a cure for every disease.
Mr. LaPage is a dangerous kidnapper inspired by the song Everyone's Gone to the Movies.
A futuristic car travels the world.
The campaign can end in the Custerdome when chaos stays low through 1944, opening a rare place of wealth and peace.
